column4: The verse says the sun does not catch the moon and night does not precede day; this gives the section's following and succession a fixed order.
The source-section root غ ش و appears in the night covering day, while day pursues it quickly; the image makes the alternation an active chase.
The verse's “إِذَا يَغْشَىٰ” makes night cover the scene, directly repeating the source-section covering verb and its sky role.
The verse's “إِذَا تَجَلَّىٰ” sets the day opening into view against the night that covers in 92:1, matching the section's paired actions.
Night is darkened and its ḍuḥā is brought forth; the passage renders the section's opening and covering as a single created transition.
The source-section root ن ف س is linked to breathing; here dawn “تَنَفَّسَ,” giving that dictionary branch a direct Quranic morning scene.
“فَالِقُ الْإِصْبَاحِ” names God as splitter of daybreak, then joins night as repose and sun and moon as reckoning; it gathers the section's dawn, cover, and measured motion.
The verse distinguishes the sun as “ضِيَاءً” and moon as “نُورًا” and gives the moon phases for reckoning, clarifying the two lights and measured sequence.
Night and day are signs: the night sign is blotted and the day sign made “مُبْصِرَةً”; this makes concealment and visibility explicit and ties them to reckoning.
God “يُكَوِّرُ” night over day and day over night, then the sun and moon each run to a term; the wrapping image directly parallels the section's exchanged light and cover.
Night and day are made “خِلْفَةً,” each succeeding the other; this gives the section's closing succession a direct formulation.
Night is made a “لِبَاسًا” and day a rising; the clothing image makes the section's night-cover and daylight-openness concrete.
Night as “لِبَاسًا” gives a direct garment image for the source-section's covering action.
Day is appointed “مَعَاشًا” after night as garment in 78:10, completing the cover-and-open pair with a distinct daytime role.
The sun is called “سِرَاجًا وَهَّاجًا,” a blazing lamp, matching the source section's sun as a source of spreading light.
The verse distinguishes moonlight, “نُورًا,” from the sun as “سِرَاجًا,” giving the section's two bodies and the sun's emitted light separate roles.
The verse calls the sun a “سِرَاجًا” and the moon “مُنِيرًا”; their paired illumination echoes the section's sun-source and moon-following scene.
The verse depicts an extended shadow, making the sun its guide; this connects the source section's revealing daylight to the changing visibility of what the light reaches.
The shadow is drawn in gradually as the sun rises over it; this gives a measured example of light changing what is covered.
Night is made for rest and day “مُبْصِرًا”; the pair directly expresses the section's covering and seeing roles.
The verse pairs a restful night with a day made “مُبْصِرًا,” stating the same concealment/visibility boundary in human terms.
The oath “وَالضُّحَىٰ” directly names the opening section's spreading morning light.
The oath by night when it settles sets the covered counterpart beside 93:1's ḍuḥā, preserving the section's paired scene.
The oath by “الشَّفَقِ” places the fading twilight boundary between daylight and the night-cover developed in the section.
Night and what it gathers (“وَاللَّيْلِ وَمَا وَسَقَ”) gives the covering half of the scene an explicit collecting action.
The oath by the moon when it is full (“إِذَا اتَّسَقَ”) matches the source-section dictionary branch linking س و ي with the moon at fullness.
Night as it departs (“إِذَا أَدْبَرَ”) continues the section's sequence from cover toward opening.
Dawn as it brightens (“إِذَا أَسْفَرَ”) supplies the light-revealing counterpart to 74:33 and the section's day scene.
The sign is night, from which day is stripped (“نَسْلَخُ مِنْهُ النَّهَارَ”), a direct image of one light giving way to another.
The sun runs to its appointed course (“تَجْرِي لِمُسْتَقَرٍّ لَهَا”), adding motion and measure to the section's ordered celestial scene.
The moon is assigned phases (“مَنَازِلَ”), a concrete account of the moon's changing position in the same ordered sky.
God brings night into day and day into night; the reciprocal entrance states the section's exchange of cover and light.
The verse again describes night entering day and day entering night, joining the alternation to God's rule over creation.
Night enters day and day enters night, while sun and moon each run to a term; this combines the section's changing light with measured celestial motion.
The verse says God makes night enter day and day enter night and subjugates sun and moon, a direct counterpart to the section's ordered succession.
Night entering day and day entering night repeats the section's exchange of covering and opening as an ongoing sign.
Sun and moon are kept in continuous service, alongside night and day; the verse gathers the same four-part cosmic order.
The sun and moon each run to an appointed term beneath the raised heavens, giving the section's recurring heavenly order a measured frame.
God alternates night and day, and the verse calls this a lesson for those who see; it makes the section's repeated transition perceptible as a sign.
The alternation of night and day is named among the signs for people of understanding, sharing the section's invitation to notice the ordered sky.
The alternation of night and day is one of God's signs, directly naming the cycle that the section stages through sun, moon, day, and night.
Night, day, sun, and moon are all subjugated for people; the verse gathers the same celestial actors into one ordered scene.
This is the question about whether people or heaven is harder to create; it supplies the creation context that 79:29 continues with night and ḍuḥā.
The heaven is raised and proportioned (“فَسَوَّاهَا”), completing the sky-building context before 79:29 turns to its night and morning.
The heaven is built and expanded, a close parallel to the whole surah's invocation of heaven and what built it.
The verse asks how the earth was spread (“سُطِحَتْ”), paralleling the source-section's secondary raised/spread dictionary sense for the 91:6 root ط ح و.
The earth is spread out (“فَرَشْنَاهَا”); this gives a direct earth-expanse counterpart to the source section's spread/raised root branch.
The earth is spread (“مَدَّ الْأَرْضَ”), a specific parallel to the section's spread-earth image in the whole surah.
The white thread of dawn becomes distinct from the black thread of night; this makes the section's light breaking through darkness a visible boundary.
The verse distinguishes ordinary clothing from “لِبَاسُ التَّقْوَىٰ”; that protective-garment metaphor directly develops the source-section root و ق ي as guarding cover.
The source-section root غ ش و is used in the verse's covering of sight, a direct transfer of the night-cover image to perception.
People fold their breasts and cover themselves with garments to hide; the shared غ ش و covering root extends the section's outside cover to inward concealment.
Evil faces are as if covered with dark pieces of night (“قِطَعًا مِنَ اللَّيْلِ مُظْلِمًا”); this makes the section's night-cover into a moral image.
The name “الْغَاشِيَةِ” uses the source-section covering root for an overwhelming event, extending the cover image to judgment.
The punishment “يَغْشَاهُم” from above and below; the source-section's covering action becomes an engulfing judgment.
The verse warns of a “غَاشِيَةٌ” from God's punishment; the section's covering root thus names a threat that can overtake a people.
Night as it recedes (“عَسْعَسَ”) supplies another exact transition from darkness toward the breathing dawn in 81:18.
The verse names ḍuḥā as a time when punishment may come while people play; it puts the section's open daylight beside danger rather than safety.
Thamud prefer blindness to guidance and are seized by humiliating punishment; this directly connects the section's opening/covering imagery to its moral and Thamud ending.
God gave Thamud the she-camel as a seeing sign (“مُبْصِرَةً”); it directly matches the section's visible sign and their response to it.
The she-camel is given as a sign and protected from harm; this supplies the fuller scene behind the section's Thamud ending.
Thamud hamstring the she-camel; the source-section's root ع ق ر for cutting the camel is used in this parallel account.
The quake seizes Thamud after they kill the camel, giving a direct account of the covering destruction associated with the section's final scene.
The she-camel has a share of water and the people a known day's share; this develops the watering arrangement surrounding the section's camel scene.
After the warning, they hamstring the camel; this parallels the source-section root ع ق ر and connects it to the announced consequence.
The cry seizes the wrongdoers after the camel is hamstrung, describing the punishment that follows the same offense.
The next verse says they were as if they had never lived there; it completes 11:67's destruction with the disappearance that the section links to annihilation.
The she-camel and people have their allotted drinking days; this is a close parallel to the camel's provision and turn in the surah's full context.
The people are warned not to touch the camel with harm; this states the boundary whose violation leads to the section's final destruction scene.
They hamstring the camel, matching the source-section root ع ق ر for the act that triggers the punishment.
The punishment seizes them after the hamstringing, directly completing the same offense-to-destruction sequence.
The she-camel is sent as a trial; the verse makes explicit the sign's testing role in the Thamud scene.
The water is apportioned between the people; this develops the provision and assigned turn around the camel.
Their companion is summoned and hamstrings the camel, matching the source-section's root ع ق ر and its singular act of violence.
The verse asks how God's punishment and warnings were, directly framing the consequence of the act in 54:29.
A single blast leaves them like dry fence trimmings; the image gives a concrete form to the section's account of destruction and leveling.
Thamud are named and “nothing was left”; this is the section's explicit parallel for annihilation after the camel episode.
The preceding reference identifies the overthrown cities that 53:54 then says were covered; it fixes the referent of that covering image.
The verse says “فَغَشَّاهَا مَا غَشَّىٰ”; the source-section root غ ش و again makes destruction a covering action, here over the overthrown cities of 53:53.
Thamud and Ad deny the overwhelming event; this places Thamud's end among the judgment scenes developed in the section.
Thamud are destroyed by the overwhelming blast (“الطَّاغِيَةِ”), a direct parallel to the section's destruction and annihilation language.
After the destruction account, the passage asks whether any remnant can be seen; it completes the no-remnant aspect also stated in 53:51.
Thamud are recalled as those who carved rock in the valley; this locates the people from the section's closing episode in another account of their history.
After the 79:27–29 sky scene, the earth is spread (“دَحَاهَا”) with a different root from source-section ط ح و; the shared feature is the created expanse, not a shared root.
The Lord of the two easts and two wests frames the repeated rising and setting boundaries that the section's changing light makes perceptible.
The verse says God made night and day from mercy so people can rest and seek bounty; it states the complementary roles staged in the section.
Sleep at night and seeking bounty by day are signs; this gives a human response to the same alternation of concealment and light.
The next scene turns to a girl buried alive; it begins the buried-child image that 81:9 completes and that parallels the section's account of hiding a daughter in earth.
The buried girl is asked for what sin she was killed; this gives the section's concealment/burial image its moral consequence.
The preceding verse describes a father's face darkening at news of a daughter; it supplies the shame that leads into the hiding and burial alternatives in 16:59.
The verse says the father may hide the girl in the dust (“يَدُسُّهُ فِي التُّرَابِ”); it is the section's direct Quranic scene for the source-section's root د س و as hiding and burying.
The verse says the self inclines toward evil except where God shows mercy; it makes the section's fujur within the nafs a concrete moral tendency, without erasing the stated counterforce of taqwa.
The oath by the self-reproaching soul names inward moral reckoning, giving the section's nafs a distinct ethical voice.
The verse describes a person wanting to persist in fujur; it uses the source-section's moral root for deliberate wrongdoing.
God guides the human being to the two ways (“النَّجْدَيْنِ”); this states the moral alternatives that the section locates within the self.
The human is shown the way and may be grateful or ungrateful; it gives another explicit formulation of moral choice corresponding to fujur and taqwa.
The verse says “قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَنْ تَزَكَّىٰ,” closely matching the source section's claim that one who purifies the self succeeds.
The next verse joins remembrance of the Lord's name with prayer to the purification in 87:14, completing that account of successful self-cultivation.
The verse asks whether the listener may purify himself; the root ز ك و directly parallels the section's self-purification.
The next verse adds taking heed, completing 80:3's possibility of purification with a response to reminder.
The person gives wealth to purify himself (“يَتَزَكَّىٰ”); this makes purification an enacted growth and cleansing, as in the source-section root ز ك و.
The verse pairs cleansing with “تُزَكِّيهِمْ”; it makes explicit the purification sense that the section gives to the source-section root ز ك و.
Giving zakat for God's face is described as being multiplied; it supports the source-section's secondary growth sense of the purification root.
The verse says God purifies whom He wills; it grounds the section's purification image in divine agency rather than self-assertion.
The righteous are in bliss, immediately before 82:14 names the wicked; this supplies one side of the moral polarity represented by the section's taqwa and fujur.
The wicked (“الْفُجَّارَ”) are in the fire, directly using the source-section's f-j-r moral branch as the counterpart to 82:13's righteous.
The record of the wicked is named with “الْفُجَّارِ”; this is another direct Quranic use of the source-section's moral root.
The root ف ج ر also describes springs bursting from rock; this concrete opening sense echoes the source-section's dawn breaking through darkness and fujur tearing a covering.
The root ف ج ر describes making a spring burst from the earth; the shared opening/gushing sense connects the section's dawn split with a different concrete image.
The earth is made to gush springs (“فَجَّرْنَا الْأَرْضَ عُيُونًا”); this gives the source-section's split/opening root a second physical scene.

The verse layers wave, wave, and cloud over darkness in the deep sea; it supplies a specific layered obscuration that extends the section's covered-light image without claiming it depicts a sun-obscuring cloud.
Noah's people cover themselves with garments while refusing to hear; the source-section covering root links bodily concealment with refusal of what is made clear.
After Thamud choose blindness and are punished in 41:17, this verse says the believers who feared God were saved; it makes the opposed outcomes explicit.
The hypothetical unending night asks who could bring light; it marks the boundary that makes the section's night/day succession a divine provision.
The hypothetical unending day asks who could bring night for rest; it states the reverse limit to the section's day/night cycle.
The rewarded faces in this verse are free of dust and humiliation, the luminous opposite of faces covered with pieces of night in 10:27.
